summary: For ages 4–6 (roughly UK Reception–Y1, US Pre-K–Grade 1; division with symbols is formalised later, e.g. US Grade 3), build division from two concrete meanings on the same quantity: equal SHARING (partitive: share 12 among 3 plates → how many each?) and equal GROUPING (quotitive: how many groups of 3 fit in 12?). Children default to sharing, so grouping must be taught deliberately — it is the bridge to repeated subtraction and to reading a times-table fact as a division. Keep quantities small, concrete, and initially remainder-free, and show the same numbers under both stories so children see one division fact (12÷3=4) pictured two ways.
misconceptions: Believing division only means sharing-out (partitive), so a 'how many groups of 3?' problem is not recognised as division at all.
Treating sharing and grouping as different operations rather than two meanings of the same ÷ — not seeing they give the same answer.
Thinking division is commutative: that 12÷3 and 3÷12 are the same (they are not).
Confusing which number is shared and which is the number of groups/size of group (dividend vs divisor) when moving to symbols.
Assuming every sharing must come out exactly and being thrown by leftovers, or sharing unequally and still calling it 'fair'.

activities.title: Share-and-group the same pile
steps: Take 12 counters and 3 plates (or hoops). Deal counters out one at a time — 'one for this plate, one for this plate, one for this plate' — until the pile is gone, then count how many each plate got (4).
On the SAME 12 counters, now scoop them into groups of 3, setting each group aside until none remain, then count how many groups you made (4).
Say the matching division sentence for both actions: 12÷3=4. Notice the same answer arrived from two completely different actions — sharing among 3, and making groups of 3.
Try a total that will not share evenly (e.g. 13 counters among 3 plates): deal fairly until you cannot give everyone one more (4 each), and name the leftover (1 left over).

Optional with an interactive counters tool: toggle between a SHARE mode (choose number of plates, tap 'deal', watch counters distribute one at a time) and a GROUP mode (choose a group size, lasso groups); flip modes on the identical pile to see the same equation form on screen.
activities.insight: Division has two meanings — equal shares and equal groups — and the same numbers can be pictured both ways, giving the same answer; this is the twin meaning children most often miss.

activities.title: Fair-share check with teddies
steps: Share 12 counters fairly between 2 teddies so each gets the same. Say how many each teddy gets (6) and explain how you know it is fair.
Count each teddy's pile and compare — are they the same, with none left over?
Describe your method: 'I gave them out one at a time to each teddy until they were gone.'
Now share the same 12 counters among 3 teddies and say how many each gets (4); then answer the matching grouping question: how many groups of 3 can you make from 12? (4) — both are 12÷3.
Try 13 counters: can you still share them fairly between the 2 teddies? What happens? (6 each with 1 left over — it won't share evenly).
activities.insight: Fairness here means everyone gets an equal amount. When the total shares evenly there are none left over, and when it does not (e.g. 13 between 2), the leftover is simply named. A child shows understanding by checking the groups match, not just by giving everyone 'some'.

activities.title: Sort the stories: sharing or grouping?
steps: Read or hear short word problems and sort each into 'sharing' (share a total among a number of people/plates) or 'grouping' (make groups of a fixed size).
Match a division sentence like 12÷3=4 to BOTH a shared picture (3 plates with 4 each) and a grouped picture (4 groups of 3).
Fill in the answer to simple remainder-free division sentences, using counters to check.
activities.insight: Both wordings — 'share among 3' and 'how many groups of 3' — are division, and a single division fact matches both a sharing picture and a grouping picture.

activities.title: Correct the unfair sharer
steps: A puppet or story character shares a set unfairly on purpose (gives one friend 'a lot'). Fix it so every friend gets an equal share.
Explain to the character why the new sharing is fair and the old one was not.
Pose and solve a fair-share dilemma aloud: 'We have 12 sweets and 4 friends — what's fair?' (3 each).
activities.insight: Talking through fairness reinforces that equal shares are the rule, while actually moving the counters is what lets the child make and check the equal shares.

checkQuestion: Here are 12 counters. Share them out fairly between these 2 teddies so each teddy gets the same. How many does each teddy get — and how do you know it's fair?
checkAnswer: 6 each — it's fair because both teddies have the same number with none left over. I gave them out one at a time to each teddy until they were gone.
